title: Biochemistry — Mixed Exam Formats (DOMiNANCE Originals)
source: KNUST Biochemistry lectures and corresponding study guides

questions.stem:
Assertion: Vitamin K deficiency may cause bleeding.
Reason: Gamma-carboxylation permits clotting factors to bind calcium.
questions.why: Vitamin K supports gamma-carboxylation of factors II, VII, IX and X, permitting calcium-dependent membrane binding and efficient coagulation. Deficiency reduces this modification, explaining the bleeding tendency.

notes.B: The calcium-binding function directly explains why loss of vitamin K-dependent carboxylation impairs clotting.
notes.C: Gamma-carboxylation does give these factors calcium-binding sites that facilitate membrane association.
notes.D: A bleeding tendency is a recognised consequence of vitamin K deficiency because several clotting proteins function poorly.
notes.E: Both the bleeding tendency and the calcium-binding role of gamma-carboxylation are established.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Heparin directly digests fibrin within an established clot.
Reason: Antithrombin neutralizes activated thrombin and factor Xa.
questions.why: Heparin accelerates inhibition of thrombin and factor Xa by antithrombin, so the reason is true. Heparin limits clot propagation, while breakdown of established fibrin requires plasmin, making the assertion false.

notes.A: Antithrombin does inhibit the activated factors, but heparin does not digest existing fibrin.
notes.B: The reason is correct because antithrombin neutralises thrombin and factor Xa, and the assertion confuses anticoagulation with fibrinolysis.
notes.C: Fibrin cleavage is a function of plasmin, so the claim that heparin digests the clot is false.
notes.E: The assertion is false, but antithrombin really does neutralise activated thrombin and factor Xa.

questions.stem:
Assertion: Platelet dense granules contain ADP and serotonin.
Reason: Platelet alpha granules contain platelet factor 4 and fibrinogen.
questions.why: Platelet dense granules store ADP and serotonin, whereas alpha granules contain proteins such as platelet factor 4 and fibrinogen. Both statements are true, but the alpha-granule inventory does not explain the separate dense-granule contents.

notes.A: The contents of alpha granules are a separate fact and do not determine which mediators dense granules store.
notes.C: Platelet factor 4 and fibrinogen are established alpha-granule components.
notes.D: Dense granules do contain ADP and serotonin, both of which participate in platelet responses.
notes.E: Both statements describe genuine components of their respective platelet granule types.

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about vitamin K and coagulation:
I. Vitamin K supports gamma-carboxylation of prothrombin.
II. Factor XIII is a vitamin K-dependent protease.
III. Citrate enhances calcium-dependent factor binding.
questions.why: Vitamin K supports prothrombin gamma-carboxylation. Factor XIIIa is a fibrin-cross-linking transglutaminase, and citrate binds free calcium, reducing its availability for coagulation.

notes.A: Factor XIIIa is a transglutaminase and citrate sequesters calcium, so the second and third statements are false.
notes.B: The prothrombin statement is correct, but factor XIII is not a vitamin K-dependent protease.
notes.C: Both selected statements are false, while vitamin K does support gamma-carboxylation of prothrombin.
notes.D: Vitamin K supports prothrombin modification, but citrate reduces rather than enhances calcium-dependent binding.

questions.stem:
Which statements about coagulation are correct?
I. Factor Xa participates in prothrombin activation.
II. Factor XIIIa cross-links fibrin strands.
III. Platelet phospholipids help organize enzyme complexes.
questions.why: Factor Xa is the catalytic component of prothrombinase, which generates thrombin. Factor XIIIa cross-links fibrin, and exposed phospholipids on activated platelets provide a surface for clotting enzyme complexes.

notes.B: This leaves out the contribution of platelet phospholipids, which support assembly of prothrombinase and other enzyme complexes.
notes.C: This leaves out the role of factor Xa, which participates in converting prothrombin to thrombin.
notes.D: This leaves out factor XIIIa, which stabilises the clot by cross-linking fibrin.
notes.E: Factor Xa is correctly included, but fibrin cross-linking and the platelet phospholipid surface also contribute to clot formation.
